cells.tense: You are here with the pen, and one cycle is closing while you stay open to the next.
cells.ask: Notice one thing today that is already finished and say it out loud before you move on.
cells.core:
Something you were making is done. Not perfect, not final, but done — the shape holds without you holding it up. You can feel the difference between pushing a thing forward and letting it stand. The next thing is already arriving, and you're meeting it from steadiness instead of scramble.

What this looks like going well: you sense when to add and when to stop adding, and you keep sensing it in real time, not after the fact. That's not a trick you learned. It's balance you keep by staying in the room with what's actually here. The next thing isn't a reward for finishing, it's just what's entering now. Stay open while it starts.
cells.sheetLine: The cycle closes. You're already open to the next.
cells.verb: closing the loop so the next one can start
cells.place: on the moving floor where you feel the weight shift and adjust before it tips

cells.tense: You are pushing toward an ending that has not arrived, calling the thing done before it has finished becoming.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you've declared complete. Leave it alone for a day and watch what it still asks of you.
cells.core:
You want the arrival more than the journey. So you close the loop early — sign the work, call the conversation settled, decide the chapter is over before it has actually ended. The bracing feels like progress. It's stepping off a moving surface because standing on it is uncomfortable.

What balance looks like here: you adjust in real time, sensing when to add and when to subtract, and you let the thing finish at its own pace. The source isn't something you force into being. It's what's entering now, and it needs your attention more than your push. Let the work stay unfinished a little longer and stay on the floor with it. Timing doesn't move faster because you want it harder.

cells.tense: You are standing at a threshold that is already behind you, treating everything as not yet arrived.
cells.ask: Tell one person about something you completed, in the past, and let them hear it without hedges.
cells.core:
The ending already happened. You keep the cycles open because letting one be over feels like losing something — a little more seeking, a little more not-yet, and every arrival becomes another search. You don't land anywhere because no landing counts.

What balance looks like: you sense what's actually here and adjust to it, instead of managing a version of events that's still in motion in your head. The way through isn't pushing your feelings back into the room. It's the source doing its work — what's entering now is already here, and you can meet it by acknowledging what already finished. One honest sentence to one person about a thing that's done. Say it when you can, and the feeling catches up.

cells.tense: You are moving through cycles without knowing which have ended and which are still turning.
cells.ask: Write down three things you've finished this year. Next to each, one word for what's next. Then close the page.
cells.core:
You're carrying some things as ongoing that are actually over. A job, a version of yourself, a conversation — done, but you keep it in the active pile because no one told you it closed. Meanwhile you treat other things as finished that are still running, and you walk away from them without noticing. The pen is down and your name is still on the page.

What balance looks like: you sense where each thing actually is and adjust, instead of running on a guess about which pile it belongs in. No one is asking for a big story about your life. Just the tally. What is complete is complete, what isn't, isn't. Letting go of what's ended isn't a loss. It's making room for the source already at the door.

A reader could reasonably say 'I don't recognize that description; my unfinished thing is financial, not emotional.' The ask still works if the read is wrong, because it's a small visible act with a finish — noticing what's already done, or naming what's over. The sentence that would serve me more than them is any line that tells them what they feel — 'you know it' or 'you're still standing in it' — so I keep their interior out of it and let the act carry the read.
